findings.summary: TR1 is closed -- the three clean READS are now pinned (measured: stat -> Optional.empty(), get -> new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[0]), and list -> ListPage.last(List.of()) are each killed by exactly theCLEANREADSReturnWhatTheDelegateHoldsAndNotAnEmptyView, 22/22 ran each time). What the new list assertion pins is that the page is NON-EMPTY and of the right SIZE; it does not pin that the decorator forwards list's three ARGUMENTS. The backing store holds only r/1 and r/2, both under the asserted prefix, there is no startAfter, and maxKeys is 10 against 2 objects -- so all three arguments are individually droppable. MEASURED, three separate mutants of the one-line body `return delegate.list(p, a, m);`, each SURVIVING all 22 tests: (1) `delegate.list("", a, m)` -- prefix ignored; (2) `delegate.list(p, null, m)` -- startAfter ignored; (3) `delegate.list(p, a, 1000)` -- maxKeys ignored. Only the argument SWAP `delegate.list(a, p, m)` dies, and it dies for the wrong reason (a null prefix throws, killing two tests including one in the streams file). The test's own comment states the broader intent -- 'list returns the delegate's page ... this is the call recovery walks the chain with' -- and mutant (1) is that intent's own failure mode in the over-broad direction: this class's javadoc argues a broken clean read is worse than a broken fault because it corrupts the control run, and a prefix-ignoring list corrupts it by returning MORE than the chain rather than less. Scoped as minor rather than major on three grounds: the RETURN is now genuinely constrained, which is the property the row claims for the read verbs; the row claims faithful ARGUMENT delegation only for put, getRange and delete, and all three are pinned (measured: `getRange(k, b, a)` and a no-op `delete` are each killed by theVerbsThatInjectNOTHINGStillDELEGATEFaithfully); and closing it is three lines inside an existing test, not a structural gap.
findings.failure_scenario: A future edit to the two-line list body that routes the wrong variable -- most plausibly dropping the prefix while adding the unreachable draw for a caller-aware fault, which M4.13's row schedules for exactly this method -- lands green. In M4.13's 1,000-seed sweep the decorator would then return every object in the store to every chain walk: other epochs' ChainEntries and the ctl/lease objects appear inside the chain being recovered, so the invariant checker sees fabricated entries and reports offset and continuity violations that no protocol code wrote. That is indistinguishable from M4.16's unsealed-ancestor I2 violation, which this row records as having cost three rounds of diagnosis already. The maxKeys mutant is the narrower version of the same thing: it makes the harness's paging behaviour differ from the delegate's, so a paging bug in recover cannot be reproduced through the injector. Closing it: seed one key OUTSIDE the prefix (e.g. `backing.putIfAbsent("x/9", body("other"))`) and assert `store.list("r/", null, 10).objects()` extracting key containsExactly("r/1", "r/2"), then one call with maxKeys=1 asserting a single object and a present nextStartAfter -- which pins all three arguments at once. If it is not closed here, it belongs on M4.13's row alongside the caller-aware-fault work that will edit this method, not lost.

findings.summary: TR2/TR3 are closed, and I verified the discrimination the new test claims rather than reading its name: `List.copyOf(injected)` -> `Collections.unmodifiableList(injected)` and `Map.copyOf(drawCounts)` -> the live `drawCounts` are EACH killed by exactly bothACCESSORSHandBackACOPYAndNotAViewOfTheirLiveState, while the equivalent copy `new TreeMap<>(drawCounts)` correctly SURVIVES -- so the test distinguishes a copy from a view and does not merely pin one implementation. The residual: the drawCounts HALF of it is vacuous in isolation. `draws` is read out of `countsBefore` itself and compared back to the same map, so the assertion holds trivially whenever the map is any snapshot at all, including an empty one. MEASURED: `drawCounts()` -> `return Map.of();` SURVIVES bothACCESSORS... entirely and is killed only by everyClassDrawsOnEVERYFaultingCallSoNoClassCanBeSKIPPEDSilently in the OTHER file. The injected() half does carry its own anti-vacuity (`hasSizeGreaterThan(size)`); the drawCounts half has none, so its non-vacuity is on loan from a different test class. Same shape in the other direction, and this one is the answer to whether the split left a deletable half: `List.copyOf` -> `new java.util.ArrayList<>(injected)` -- a genuine copy that is MUTABLE -- survives bothACCESSORS... and is killed only by theInjectedRecordIsASNAPSHOTACallerCannotMutate in FaultInjectingStoreTest.java:253. So the two tests pin strictly different halves of one line and NEITHER is redundant, even though the newer one's name ('hands back a COPY and not a VIEW') reads as a superset of the older one's ('is a SNAPSHOT a caller cannot mutate'). The new test's comment does cross-reference the older one by test name, which mitigates it; it does not name the file.
findings.failure_scenario: Two concrete paths. (1) A tidy-up that reads bothACCESSORS... as subsuming theInjectedRecordIsASNAPSHOT... and deletes the latter re-opens `List.copyOf` -> `new ArrayList<>` silently: injected() then hands the sweep an editable copy of the only evidence it has about which faults fired, and a caller can forge or drop an Injected record with nothing failing. Measured: that mutant has exactly one killing test today. (2) If everyClassDraws... is ever narrowed -- its containsExactlyInAnyOrderEntriesOf map is the count the row itself says M4.13 will edit -- drawCounts() becomes free to return an empty or stale map with bothACCESSORS... still green, and the accessor half then proves nothing: a phase comparison over an always-empty map reports 'no change' having compared nothing, which is verbatim the silent-simulator failure that test exists to prevent. One line closes it: assert `store.drawCounts().getOrDefault("unreachable", 0)` is `draws + 1` after the second fault, mirroring the `hasSizeGreaterThan(size)` the injected half already carries.

answer_to_author: Pass. TR1 is dead and I measured it three ways rather than reading the new test's name: stat -> Optional.empty(), get -> a zero-byte stream, and list -> an empty page are each killed by theCLEANREADSReturnWhatTheDelegateHoldsAndNotAnEmptyView and by nothing else, which is the right shape -- every other read-back in the suite goes to the backing store, and this is the only test that observes the decorator's own reads. TR2/TR3 are dead the same way, and the copy-versus-view distinction is real rather than nominal: the unmodifiable-view and live-map mutants both die, and `new TreeMap<>(drawCounts)` -- an equivalent copy -- correctly survives, so the test constrains the property and not the constructor chosen for it. FaultFixtures does NOT need a test of its own, and the extraction is constrained by construction rather than by argument: `body` -> a same-length zeroed array is killed by 8 tests across all THREE classes, and `read` -> a constant by 5 across two. A test of body() would have to assert that a Body carries the bytes handed to it, which is the accessor-echo shape M4.3's own row already records as coverage rather than verification -- the three classes are the stronger check, and they are stronger precisely because the fixture is shared. I re-measured 13 of the earlier kills through the extraction and both splits and none regressed: ambiguous putIfAbsent landing -> `delegate.put` (clobbers the slot owner), ambiguous putIfMatch landing -> unconditional `put`, each of putIfMatch's two result-discarding draws deleted, scramble -> `seed * 3 + stream`, duplicateDraws aliased onto stream 1, the probability guard body deleted, the unreachable key blanked, getRange bounds swapped, delete made a no-op, the clean putIfAbsent writing a same-length zeroed array, the clean putIfMatch dropping its version, and the duplicate retry deleted -- 13 mutants, 13 kills, each named by a test in the file where the seam says it should live. The one mutant I found that survives and is DISCLOSED is the countDraw label swap (ambiguousPut <-> duplicatePut), which the javadoc and the row both call unobservable; I confirmed it survives all 22 and confirmed why, which is that the asymmetric-mix map is 7/4/4 and the two swapped classes are both 4. On the three seams after two splits: they are coherent -- what a fault does to a caller, which stream a class draws from, what the injector does when it is not injecting -- and every mutant I ran was killed by a test in the file its seam predicts, with no cross-file surprises. The one hazard the split created is TR5's, and it is worth one sentence in the commit body rather than a fix: the two halves of `List.copyOf` now sit in different files with one killing test each, the newer name reads as a superset of the older, and deleting the older re-opens a live mutant. Both findings are minors and rule 11 says fixing them here is usually wrong -- round 13 on this task has spent several rounds on prose surface added by the previous round's fix. Record them: TR4 in the row's NOT-covered list, or on M4.13, whose own row already schedules the edit to `list` that would trip it.
